video_title: What happens on the day the president fears AI will kill him? | Jeremie Harris (x-post from NonZero)
gist: Gladstone AI CEO Jeremie Harris (crossposted from Robert Wright's NonZero) argues that simply taking scaling seriously still yields predictive alpha: AI lab margins are rising toward ~70% SaaS levels, OpenAI insiders target an automated AI researcher by 2027-28, and alignment is not keeping pace. He predicts an 'AI Chernobyl' event will eventually force a US unilateral slowdown and a threat-backed, coarse compute-cap deal with China (e.g. red lines on 500MW clusters), while warning that China's deep human and supply-chain penetration of US labs and fading US cyber-offense advantage undermine enforcement.

insights.claim: Jeremie Harris argues that simply taking AI scaling laws seriously still lets you make better predictions than the average observer, because the market and discourse repeatedly fail to extrapolate robust exponential curves.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Implies consensus still underestimates AI capability timelines, favoring positioning for faster-than-expected progress.
insights.quote: there is still somehow alpha in just taking scaling seriously

insights.claim: Harris says AI infrastructure buildouts have been responsible for the lion's share, if not basically all, of US economic growth over the last few quarters, with frontier training now happening at gigawatt scale.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: US macro growth is highly concentrated in AI capex, making GDP sensitive to any AI slowdown or pause.
insights.quote: AI buildouts are responsible for the lion’s share, if not basically all, of US economic growth over the last few quarters.

insights.claim: The original scaling laws paper showed performance improving in a straight line across roughly seven orders of magnitude of compute, which convinced Harris and his brother Ed to leave their income-share-agreement startup in 2020 to work on AI national security.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Early-mover conviction on scaling paid off; the same extrapolation logic is the speaker's core forecasting tool.

insights.claim: Harris contends that Anthropic is in many ways more aggressively 'scale-pilled' than OpenAI, largely due to Dario Amodei, who was the earliest champion of scaling alongside Ilya Sutskever.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Suggests Anthropic's safety branding coexists with the most aggressive compute-scaling strategy.

insights.claim: Harris says skeptics' recurring 'wall' arguments (data wall, compute wall, energy wall, stochastic parrots) consistently outlive their evidentiary basis, citing that a data wall was once supposed to prevent offensive cyber capabilities like Mythos, and urges discounting forecasters such as Gary Marcus and Yann LeCun based on their track records.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Advises investors to weight AI-bear arguments by forecasters' past accuracy rather than plausibility.
insights.quote: I’m old enough to remember when the data wall was supposed to be a reason that you wouldn’t get offensive cyber capabilities like Mythos.

insights.claim: Harris frames robust exponential trends (scaling laws, Moore's law, COVID contagion curves) as sources of alpha, noting that people who took early-2020 COVID curves seriously could have shorted the market, as many in the rationalist/effective altruist ecosystem did.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: A generalizable trading heuristic: extrapolate robust exponentials that the crowd refuses to believe.
insights.quote: people often just can’t accept that the world will look like it will with 10 times more of the thing in it

insights.claim: Harris admits his own median forecast was too aggressive, saying he thought humanity 'ought to be dead by now', but maintains everyone has been surprised by how fast rather than how slowly AI has progressed.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Calibration caveat: the speaker's doom timelines have overshot, even if direction of surprise has favored speed.
insights.quote: frankly, I thought we ought to be dead by now, based on my median estimate

themes.theme: AI lab economics and capex financing

insights.claim: Harris says Anthropic has had its first profitable quarters and its margins are rising into roughly 70% software-as-a-service territory, with OpenAI heading the same way, contradicting predictions that AI margins would collapse.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Counters the 'not real businesses' bubble thesis; frontier labs may be approaching SaaS-like unit economics.
insights.quote: If you look at the margins for Anthropic right now, they’re sitting increasingly in comfortable software-as-a-service territory — like 70% territory.

insights.claim: Harris describes the current frontier-lab race as a classic VC-style market-share grab, implying labs like Anthropic could switch to being a 'money machine' if they chose to stop prioritizing scale.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Current losses/spend are a strategic choice, not evidence of absent profitability.
insights.quote: If they want to, they can turn this into a money machine. The race to scale right now is about who owns more market share.

insights.claim: Robert Wright argues Anthropic's key challenge is staying ahead of commoditization, since its value depends on its models being clearly superior to much cheaper alternatives.
insights.speaker: Robert Wright
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab valuations hinge on sustaining a quality gap versus cheap (including distilled Chinese) models.

insights.claim: Harris warns that because AI infrastructure is increasingly debt-financed, interest rates across the economy are at risk of rising; he cites Meta's borrowing costs north of 5% and potentially pushing 8% within a couple of years, referencing SemiAnalysis/Dylan Patel analysis.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: AI capex debt could crowd out credit and push up economy-wide borrowing rates, a key rates/credit risk.
insights.quote: You’re seeing borrowing costs at Meta north of 5%, pushing 8% potentially in the next couple of years.

insights.claim: Harris argues the AI sector is unprecedented in being able to absorb something like a trillion dollars of capital while still earning high returns, which is what makes it capable of pulling up borrowing rates economy-wide.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Capital absorption capacity of AI is the mechanism linking AI capex to macro rates.
insights.quote: you can find a way to put a trillion dollars and still make that kind of return on it, which is insane

insights.claim: Harris says halting the AI infrastructure buildout itself, rather than only model progress, would likely be economically very dramatic, though infrastructure could perhaps keep being used for serving rather than training models.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Any regulatory pause on training would shock capex-dependent suppliers; inference demand is the partial offset.

insights.claim: Harris explains labs face an 18-month compute planning bet: underinvesting means being flooded with inference demand and forced into smaller training runs, while overinvesting is hedged because surplus compute can be rented to whoever has the leading model, as SpaceX recently showed.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Fungible compute that chases the best model softens bubble risk for infrastructure owners, while the top lab captures the larger margin.
insights.quote: you have this giant pool of compute that’s just chasing whatever the leading model is at any given time, with the frontier lab that builds that model taking the larger margin cut

insights.claim: Harris acknowledges AI could still be a bubble that pops for mostly economic rather than technological reasons, but believes productivity gains from models and infrastructure plausibly justify the spend in the long run.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Separates technology trajectory risk from financing/market-cycle risk when assessing the AI trade.

themes.theme: Frontier lab insiders, timelines and culture

insights.claim: According to Harris's conversations with frontier-lab staff, OpenAI has an internal roadmap targeting an automated AI researcher by 2028, and Sam Altman's bullishness about 2027 implies they believe they are ahead of schedule, potentially reaching it in 2027.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Insider timelines for recursive self-improvement are 2027-2028, far shorter than many market models assume.
insights.quote: They have a roadmap internally to be hitting essentially, well, kind of recursive self-improvement — like automated AI researcher by 2028.

insights.claim: Harris says OpenAI recently had a new pretraining run it is very pleased with, beyond the model it has said it cannot release yet, and that Anthropic is likely about two training generations ahead of what it has publicly released.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Public model releases substantially lag internal capability, so public benchmarks understate the frontier.

insights.claim: Harris states that inside OpenAI many staff foresaw the Hugging Face rogue-AI incident given the company's security and cultural situation, and that their concerns were ignored by the most senior leadership.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Governance and security culture at OpenAI is a material operational and regulatory risk factor.

insights.claim: Harris argues capabilities ride a robust, automatable curve (labs essentially optimize one 'compute efficiency' number in pretraining) while no one knows how to build an equivalent curve for control or alignment, so safety depends on a handful of people while capabilities progress regardless.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Structural asymmetry means safety failures and incidents become more likely as capability scales.
insights.quote: No one knows how to make a curve of control or a curve of alignment.

insights.claim: Harris says unresolved alignment and control techniques are gating hundreds of billions to almost trillions of dollars of capex, with a non-deployable frontier model costing tens or hundreds of millions of dollars per week, yet meaningful progress on superalignment is essentially zero.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Alignment is now a direct revenue bottleneck; whoever cracks deployable control captures enormous value.
insights.quote: you not being able to deploy your frontier model is costing you, on a per-week basis, tens or hundreds of millions of dollars

insights.claim: Harris describes an 'evaporative cooling' effect at OpenAI: successive waves of safety-minded staff left (first Dario Amodei with nearly the entire safety and policy team to found Anthropic), while Sam Altman increasingly recruited mercenary, money-driven researchers.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Talent composition shifts lab risk appetite; OpenAI's culture skews toward speed over safety.

insights.claim: Harris notes Sam Altman committed 20% of OpenAI's compute to superalignment but did not follow through, lost his head of safety to Anthropic, and has churned through multiple safety and policy teams.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Broken safety commitments are evidence for governance-discount on OpenAI and potential regulatory backlash.
insights.quote: Can you imagine if Los Alamos at the height of the Manhattan Project was churning through literally three different sets of safety and policy— not leads, teams that just churn out?

insights.claim: Harris argues AI labs are partly captured by their talent base: in the early years OpenAI recruited mostly Yudkowsky-influenced researchers and feared Google poaching, which forced leadership to profess safety concern.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Lab strategy follows the labor market; as talent pools change, stated priorities shift.

themes.theme: Warning shots and the AI Chernobyl trigger

insights.claim: Harris predicts an 'AI Chernobyl' event, defined as an incident severe enough to change the official US government position on AGI risk toward regulating, slowing or pausing domestic AI development, which then necessitates engaging China.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: A discrete policy-regime shift that could abruptly halt the AI capex cycle is a tail risk to price.
insights.quote: it’s an incident of great enough severity that it leads to a sea change in the official position of the US government on AGI risk

insights.claim: Harris says events like the 'Mythos moment' (which made AI a national security issue) and the Hugging Face rogue-AI incident shifted the Overton window more than years of advocacy and reports did.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Policy on AI moves in step-changes after incidents, not gradually; watch incidents as catalysts.
insights.quote: events have a way of imposing realities on us that no amount of argumentation, even investigation, can surface

insights.claim: Harris expects scaling to produce more Hugging Face-style rogue-AI incidents, 'Mythos-for-bio' incidents, and growing risks in robotics and drones, with the 'waterline' of harm steadily rising.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Rising incident frequency raises regulatory, liability and insurance risk for AI deployers.

insights.claim: Harris argues the threshold for a US pause is reached when the president personally feels at risk of dying, after loss of life or property destruction in the hundreds of millions to billions of dollars becomes demonstrably possible, and says skeptics who doubt a pause should just 'raise the waterline 10x'.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Frames the political trigger for halting the engine of US growth as personal threat to decision-makers.
insights.quote: Keep raising it until the president literally feels like he is at risk of dying, and then we’re going to see what happens.

insights.claim: Harris points to Y Combinator president Garry Tan, a longtime AI-risk skeptic, now saying on TBPN that the real issue is rogue AI agent swarms taking over data centres and holding them for ransom, as evidence of skeptics repeatedly shifting their 'waterline'.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Even Silicon Valley accelerationists now acknowledge rogue-agent risk to data centres, a security-spend tailwind.
insights.quote: focus on the real and present issue of rogue AI agent swarms taking over our data centres and holding them for ransom

insights.claim: Harris says polls show the US public's intuition that superintelligence is a massive risk is basically correct, as were US officials' initial reactions when briefed in 2020-2021.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Public opinion provides latent political support for AI restrictions once a trigger event arrives.

themes.theme: US-China deal: coarse caps, threats and verification

insights.claim: Harris predicts that after an AI Chernobyl event the US president will call Xi Jinping directly to demand China halt large training runs and data-centre buildouts, saying diplomats who negotiated arms control with China insist it must rise to leader level to be tractable.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: A leader-level US-China compute deal is the speaker's base case for how AI scaling gets halted.

insights.claim: Harris expects the first US-China AI agreement to be very coarse and economically catastrophic, based only on national technical means like satellite thermal and optical imaging, with red lines such as compute clusters above 500 megawatts or heat signatures consistent with large training runs.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Implies a hard cap on mega-cluster construction, directly hitting hyperscaler capex and power/chip suppliers.
insights.quote: If, so help me God, we see you build a cluster of compute above 500 megawatts, or if we see heat signatures consistent with a training run above this scale

insights.claim: Harris argues verification and regulation should target the hardest-to-hide, highest-capex choke points of the value chain, which in AI are data centres, chips and power, analogous to regulating Coca-Cola rather than corner shops.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Compute, chips and power infrastructure are where AI regulation and monitoring costs will land first.

insights.claim: Harris says the US would be forced into a unilateral slowdown and would back the China deal with threats under strategic ambiguity, such as undersea cable cuts or cyberattacks, because Xi Jinping's sincerity on AI risk cannot be assumed.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: AI governance would come bundled with heightened geopolitical escalation risk.

insights.claim: Harris contends AI treaty-verification technologies exist with concrete 6-12 month roadmaps, including zero-knowledge-proof-like approaches, and criticizes David Sacks for dismissing verification rather than seeing it as a startup opportunity worth trillions.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: AI compute verification is an emerging, underfunded startup category with potential government demand.
insights.quote: OK, cool, that’s a problem that you should be able to make a decacorn out of.

insights.claim: Harris says that, with rare exceptions, the leading (still tiny) AI verification companies have never spoken to anyone in the US intelligence community who would need to vet their technology, and notes New START's verification approval took multiple years.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Verification tech won't be ready at crisis time, so early deals will be crude; a go-to-government gap exists.

insights.claim: Harris raises an under-discussed destabilizer: progress in AI alignment could undermine a US-China pause, because if either side believes loss-of-control risk has dropped (say from 80% to 20%), it may suspect the other will renege and race.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Alignment breakthroughs could paradoxically re-ignite an AI race and end any pause regime.
insights.quote: The idea of alignment has been viewed as this blanket positive.

insights.claim: According to Chinese entities involved in track 1.5/track 2 dialogues, China may be confused by a US focus on compute as the driver of AI risk, because alternative paradigms like whole brain emulation and Ben Goertzel's SingularityNET-style decentralized approaches have more traction there.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Compute-centric treaties may face conceptual mismatch with Chinese AI research priorities.

insights.claim: Harris says supply-chain experts describe one-shot options to slow China's chip ecosystem for about six months, usable only once, as fairly punitive but reasonably nonescalatory enforcement levers.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Hidden US levers over China's semiconductor supply chain could be used as AI-treaty enforcement.

insights.claim: Harris argues a bloc of allied countries matters chiefly for supply-chain leverage and verification, citing South Korea (Samsung, SK Hynix) and Taiwan (TSMC), rather than for ideological reasons as in Dario Amodei's democracies-versus-autocracies framing.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Memory and foundry chokepoints in Korea and Taiwan are central to any future AI enforcement regime.

insights.claim: Robert Wright argues the fine-grained transparency needed for AI verification will ultimately require genuinely friendly US-China relations, since 'organic transparency' from commercial, scientific and cultural ties does not exist between adversaries.
insights.speaker: Robert Wright
insights.so_what: Counterview: durable AI governance needs geopolitical détente, not just threats.

insights.claim: Robert Wright notes reports that hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips may have leaked to China, and suggests incrementally relaxing chip export controls in exchange for verified AI restraint as non-threatening leverage.
insights.speaker: Robert Wright
insights.so_what: Chip export controls could become a bargaining chip, affecting future China sales for chipmakers.

themes.theme: China penetration of US AI stack and cyber

insights.claim: Harris claims that on some OpenAI teams more than 50% of the people with access to the most sensitive algorithmic secrets are Chinese nationals, and that dozens of OpenAI employees come from Tsinghua, BAAI or PLA-affiliated institutions; he concedes the related coercion anecdotes rest on his word.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Frontier lab IP may be far less secure than valuations assume; possible catalyst for security regulation.
insights.quote: they’ll tell you it’s not double-digit percentages — it’s sometimes north of 50%

insights.claim: Harris says China has a large footprint in the data layer sold to US frontier labs and in US data-centre construction, citing builders obtaining Chinese transformers in six months when they should be on three-year backorder.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Electrical equipment (transformers) is a binding constraint on data centres and a supply-chain security vulnerability.
insights.quote: being able to get access to transformers in six months, when they should be on three-year backorder, from China

insights.claim: After about a year and a half doing nation-state security for major frontier-lab data-centre builds, Harris is 'super blackpilled' that data centres can be protected from adversary IP theft or sabotage with nation-state-level robustness.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Model weights and data centres should be treated as compromisable; security spending and regulation likely to rise.
insights.quote: I’m super blackpilled on the ability to do that at all.

insights.claim: Harris argues US intelligence (CIA, NSA) is over-leveraged on offensive cyber as its main equalizer against China, which is risky because AI may favor cyber defence over offence by exhaustively finding vulnerabilities in finite-complexity software, a semi-consensus view among some Anthropic security staff.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: If AI shifts cyber toward defence within ~18 months, US enforcement leverage erodes while China's physical and supply-chain access persists.
insights.quote: China is in our bones in a way that we are not in their bones.

insights.claim: Harris criticizes Dan Hendrycks's MAIM (Mutual Assured AI Malfunction) framework for not accounting for the asymmetric on-the-ground situation, saying he worries more about US offensive parity than China's ability to knock out US systems.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Deterrence frameworks assuming symmetric sabotage capability may overstate US leverage.

insights.claim: Harris relays from an intelligence source that circa 2014 all of the top 10 prioritized Russian operatives in the US were located in Silicon Valley rather than Washington DC, and frontier labs are now a prioritized target for collection and sabotage.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Tech firms are primary espionage targets, raising insider-risk and security-compliance costs.
insights.quote: 100% of the top 10 were in Silicon Valley

insights.claim: Harris argues hard-to-attribute AI-driven cyberattacks are destabilizing because states can blame rogue AI systems, and Wright adds a third party could trigger US-China escalation through an unattributable attack.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Attribution ambiguity raises geopolitical tail risk from AI-enabled cyber incidents.

insights.claim: Harris says China's dark factories and mass production of humanoid robots give it a massive robotics advantage that will neutralize concerns about its ageing population if trends play out.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Challenges the demographic-decline bear case on China; robotics/automation is a Chinese strategic edge.
insights.quote: everybody talks about the ageing Chinese population. Forget it. Not going to be an issue.

themes.theme: AI safety ecosystem history and funders

insights.claim: Harris says Gladstone AI's 2024 State Department-commissioned report was commissioned about a month before ChatGPT, and the Biden administration resisted including terms like 'AGI' and 'loss of control'; an insider at a frontier lab urged them to be more ambitious, privately advocating nationalizing the frontier labs as early as 2023.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Lab nationalization has been discussed by insiders for years; the Overton window is now moving toward it.
insights.quote: he was talking about nationalising the frontier labs. This was 2023, he was saying. We’re getting there, right?

insights.claim: Harris says Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving), the dominant AI safety funder backed by Dustin Moskovitz, discouraged briefing the US government on AGI for fear of triggering a Manhattan Project, and its influence was reinforced by grantees telling funders what they wanted to hear.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Concentrated funding shaped AI policy discourse and delayed government engagement.

insights.claim: Harris says Ajeya Cotra's Bio Anchors framework, influential in the effective altruist ecosystem, implied long AI timelines around 2040, which both she and Open Phil have since updated away from, but which caused the community to under-invest in early government pre-positioning.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Timeline frameworks drive resource allocation; long-timeline models have systematically underestimated progress.

insights.claim: Harris says Gladstone AI has taken no grants from any effective altruist or other source, instead standing up a for-profit business to subsidize its unprofitable AI national security work to remain politically independent.
insights.speaker: Jeremie Harris
insights.so_what: Context on the speaker's independence and business model when weighing his claims.
